review_text_raw:
Cheap and easy adventure game, but not really a puzzle game. 

The game is fun for what it is, but it isn't what I expected at all. When I fired it up I thought it was going to be a much deeper experience. That isn't to say it wasn't enjoyable, it at the very minimum had some amazing atmosphere and music. It was fun for a bit to read through old IRC chat logs and relive its heyday. 

Most of the game is following instructions without question. This was never subverted, and everything was as simple as expected throughout the entire game. I was expecting a few missions where I edited records, or deleted files, to backfire, and I would have to restore those records or find another copy of the file, but nothing of the sort happened. I instead became super hackerman within 2 hours and with some software I downloaded I was able to break into just about every computer on the planet. The game in general isn't particularly hard, and if you know anything about unix commands, you can get through everything fairly quickly. If you lose or someone traces you the worst that happens is you reboot your virtual computer, and the most you lose out is some time but that is about it, so the stakes are about as low as possible. 

There were a few bugs, and few missions never triggered unless I followed a guide. That is the only reason I have 8 hours on the game, I beat it easily doing just about everything except the DLC in around 4 hours. It took me redoing a particular part twice to get the /el message board missions to trigger but if you ignore 100% completion read quickly, know your unix commands and stick to the main story, you can finish even faster.

I do have a few gripes though, for one the user tags at the moment say it is a simulation and programming game. However this can't be further from the truth. The tutorial at first used real unix commands to control your computer, and I was preparing for a much more "hardcore experience". However, the more that I played the more that I was disappointed with the puzzles. It took me until about an hour in before I realized it isn't a puzzle game at all. It really just an adventure game. Very few locks have time pressure and that is the hardest part of the game. Otherwise you just follow instructions and don't really think about what is going on.  The simulation aspects are fairly shallow, and at most the "hacking" is just run multiple programs, one after another. There is no programming at all, and I have no idea how why that is a tag. I think that some people misinterpret the terminal as programming. The terminal is something most people used to interact with computers up until the late 90s, and if you use Linux, you use it pretty much every day. Its just an alternate interface, it would be like calling using a mouse programming.

Pick it up on a deep sale if you want to kill some time, but there are other games that are much deeper and have more going on. The atmosphere is nice, and snooping through old IRC logs is worth the nostalgia alone, but if you have no interest in that, I would recommend for you to pass on this.

review_text_raw:
[h1] INTRO [/h1]
The best way to describe Hacknet for me is that it's an experience. You will like it if you're curious about what you see in the trailers and on YouTube. The comparison to real hacking that I've seen around the Interwebs is there in the similarities with the commands that you type into a terminal window, and the use of I.P. addresses, but that's really about it (Read about that here: https://www.quora.com/How-closely-is-HackNet-OS-game-related-to-the-real-life-hacking). But besides all of that, you should give it a go. It's $15, and it was worth every dime. I'll go into details below about why, but I would blanket recommend this game if you've seen anything interesting in the trailers, reviews, or content about this game. 

[h1] BEGINNING [/h1]
I'll go chronologically here: I found this game in a weird way. I found Furi through Dunkey's Best of 2017, and while listening to the Soundtrack for it Payload came on thanks to shuffle. I'll get to the soundtrack a "Bit" later, but Payload is one heck of an advertisement for Hacknet. The developer Matt Trobbiani said that the tutorial was what he was most proud of, which comes right when you start a New Session (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=suQ_dT8ucVg 0:52). I found that it was... lacking. I was unsure of how to solve most problems at the beginning of the game that I was presented with, and the convoluted explanations of what the commands did was not helpful for knowing what exactly to do with them. My examples here are the explanation of Shells and an Executable that I can't remember. If you're anything like me, the first hour(s) will be a grind: learning the commands, getting a feel for what the missions are asking of you, and learning the flow of the game. [i] Note: I found that saying what's wrong plainly will help with finding a solution. For example: "My file got deleted, I need another one. I'll just go and steal it". [/i] This was my challenge, and I found myself on the incredibly helpful Steam guide more than a few times in the early game (DO NOT USE THIS UNTIL YOU ARE STUCK https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=499723234). This was a more sufficient tutorial for getting accustomed to the game and progressing. But that's just the beginning of the game, and the game's biggest fault in my opinion. 

[h1] MID GAME [/h1]
After my mixed experience with the beginning of the game, things got better, and quickly. After you know the commands well and how they are used, (shell, rm, probe, connect, addnote, append/replace, upload, and a few more basics) you start to see the timing the game expects of you. The Trace adds real intensity to the game that will the expanded upon later. It really gets exciting as the commands come naturally to you. I disagree with Matt about the success of the tutorial, rather I would praise him on the pacing and creativity of the mid and the beautiful, beautiful, oh so beautiful endgame. I found myself going back to the guide less and less, and realizing that most problems can be solved with basic knowledge of the game, and a curiosity for combing through systems. You've got to look carefully through everything. You'll find everything from weird conversations to passwords that you can't proceed without. The flow of the mid game is quite enjoyable as the difficulty slowly picks up and your Net Map gets bigger and bigger. You start to get the sense that Hacknet is an open world game, which it is. Hacknet takes you through the mid game and cleverly prepares you for the final challenges that you will be ready for if you've paid attention throughout the game, and you won't have to use any guides at all. 

[h1] ENDGAME [/h1]
Hacknet's final challenge is daunting, but well-designed. Now for the ending. I won't say too much because it is best experienced without expectation, but I will say that it made it all worth it. Learning the commands, how the game is played, it all comes together. In a rather mild game, the experience of the ending is quite "shocking". This was where Hacknet was completely untouchable. I would give any amount of money to go back and experience that ending for the first time again. Best part of the game, by far. Sequencer is my favorite Executable and it will be yours as well once you finish the game. Now to the soundtrack, because this section and the next one go hand-in-hand. 

[h1] MUSIC [/h1]
Now I'm a music guy, and the soundtrack plays a huge role in Hacknet's overall experience. That's because there are almost no sound effects, the beeping of the Trace timer, accepting and competing contracts, and an Incoming Signal are all of the ones I can think of right now. If you turned the music off in settings, the game would be silent. Therefore there is a huge emphasis on the soundtrack. And I'll just say that I'm listening to Roja Drifts By just to get in the spirit for this section. There's a few really good ones, and the rest are ok. Here's a list of the good stuff: Carpenter Brut for obvious reasons, Tetrameth, Roja Drifts By, Outrun the Wolves, and in Labyrinths Dream Head, and even the legendary Resonance makes an appearance (at one point Matt said he thought he wouldn't make enough money to pay the artists back). The rest of the soundtrack was nice and "techno-y" and perfectly fit with the theme of the game and what you see on your screen. But the standout for me was obviously Remi Gallego. Everything he's put out, especially for Hacknet and Labyrinths turned out to be some of my favorite songs ever. Payload, Panic Track (which is basically Malware Injection), ClearText, and Sabotage were all masterpiece songs. I encourage you to check out the work he did on Hell is Other Demons as well if you liked his stuff here, it's great. However mentioning Payload gives me the opportunity to talk about the one problem that Hacknet has with its use of the soundtrack. I know Payload appears in Labyrinths, but the problem occurs in the main game as well. The songs are just set to repeat until you complete a contract or two (I also did not appreciate Matt cutting out the glitching in Payload, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4l6arwAIA6w 4:03). It gets old, and I found myself muting the music for a while to keep all of the tracks fresh because they are reused at points. 

[h1] STORY [/h1]
Lastly I'll touch on the story here, it's good. There's a Bit of a twist as to the fate of Hacknet which I thought was really cool, but it was also a bit convoluted. Took me some reading afterwards to figure out what just happened, but that's also because I wasn't really paying attention to the story and more worrying about why I couldn't complete some mission. Let's just say it's not spelled out, but I guess some players understood it pretty easily (THIS IS A STEAM FORUM ABOUT THE ENDING AND EXPLAINING IT, I AM ONLY INCLUDING IT TO SHOW THAT THE ENDING IS EXPLAINED IF YOU LOOK FOR IT https://steamcommunity.com/app/365450/discussions/0/530649887207612803/). Anyways, the story is strong and interesting, but you don't play it for the story. It's interesting enough that you could, but you just don't. 

[h1] SUMMARY & RATING [/h1]
Overall an unforgettable experience. Easter eggs, music, intensity, it's fun for the whole family (not really suitable for the whole family). Be patient in the beginning, learn the commands, comb through the systems, learn what is required of you. There are bumps and surprises waiting for you, and you're rewarded for jumping through each hurdle. Please give this a shot, I found music that I loved, an ending so good I pooped myself, I fought my way through an unfamiliar system, and I learned about video games. There's bound to be something you like about the game if you [b] stick with it [/b]. And if you liked what you played in the main game, get Labyrinths (https://store.steampowered.com/app/521840/Hacknet__Labyrinths/). You won't be sorry, mate. Matt put a lot of love into this game, and it shows. [b] 9/10. [/b]

review_text_raw:
Cool Concept, But It Couldn’t Keep Me Hooked

Hacknet starts strong. The idea of diving into a terminal-based hacking sim with a mysterious narrative hook is instantly appealing, especially if you’re into cyberpunk aesthetics or want to feel like a digital detective. At first, typing out real commands and navigating the virtual systems feels immersive and fresh. But that feeling didn’t last long for me.

The main problem is how quickly the novelty wears off. After a couple of missions, the gameplay loop becomes repetitive — scan, probe, crack, read a few emails, rinse and repeat. There’s little variety or meaningful evolution in the mechanics. You’re not solving clever puzzles so much as going through the motions of the same routine over and over.

The story, while intriguing in concept, never really grabbed me. It’s told in fragments through logs and emails, but it lacks emotional weight or urgency. I never felt particularly invested in the characters or their motivations — and a lot of the writing just felt flat.

On top of that, there are some pacing issues. Some tasks feel tedious and drawn out, while others jump ahead abruptly. And if you’re not already familiar with basic command-line structure, the early learning curve can feel more frustrating than fun.

I really wanted to like Hacknet. It nails the aesthetic and tone, and I respect the ambition. But the shallow gameplay and underwhelming story made it feel more like a tech demo than a fully satisfying experience.

review_text_raw:
To be fair Uplink is better. This game is good because you get to use the keyboard. Uplink is a hacking game where keyboard is not used, so the biggest flaw is now solved. Problem is the game lacks a bit of adrenaline. 

1) Most servers don't trace you, so you can just hang around forever.
2) Its not clear where you are connected too. Once you hack a place is there opened forever. You don't even have to disconnect.
3) You clear your logs but not the disconnected log, which makes no sense. In Uplink you have to clear logs at origin and destination, seems more realistic.
4) Its too easy to go up the ranking. 
5) In Uplink you had money to worry about. Upgrade hardware and buy software. In Hacknet all you get is reputation, that also have no impact besides gettings invitations.
6) The game does not allow you to accept more than 1 mission.
7) The storyline is a bit broken. I made 1 mission that lead to a hacker invading my computer, that leads to another mission and to another mission and basically you cannot accept other mission while the "story" is leading you in 1 way. That made me join an organization and now I cannot finish the old missions. Basically I lost 3 missions, cannot be played.
8) The game UI is a bit limited. I cannot open a file and an email at the same time. Which makes very annoying to take note to things. Althought I cannot complain much on that, as in Uplink I really had a pen and paper next to me all the time, in this game I never used real paper so far.
9) Uplink allow you to do other stuff, such as Stock Market, browse any server, etc. Hacknet is limited. You only get the servers IP when the game wants you to get. There is not freedom besides follow the story.
10) Uplink allows you to choose which mission to make, in the sense of choosing to be a good or a bad hacker. In Hacknet some missions presentation don't have more than 2 lines. You have to accept missions without even knowing what skills you need, what tools you need and what you have to do. Its really 1 path only. And if you try to get missions in different orders you lose them, just like I lost 3. UPDATE: Because of this 1 path only + cannot accept more than 1 mission, you can game over all the time. If you delete the wrong file, edit the wrong record, its finished. People call this bug in the forum, I call this lack of flexibility. In Uplink you could simply give up on a mission and pay a fine. If you delete a file you are suppose to upload, it shouldn't be game over, just some kind of punishment.
11) It uses Unix commands but limit them. For instance you have rm command but cannot be used to delete folders. Cannot download folders either.
12) Find it a bit weird that no special software is required to know when you are being traced.
13) So far the challenge of the game seems to be more about curiosity of the player. Meaning you have to look into every folder and file and read and see what you can find (be aware) rather than having a challenge on the hacking it self, such as limited time, required software, go throught LAN networks, etc.
14) You can hack a webserver, a main frame, a home pc or a cell phone, they all look the same, they all have same file structure, they are all hacked with same tools. A bit boring no?
15) Network map completely unecessary. Its just a harder way to find servers, if you are not going to use it to bounce like Uplink, why have that? Just a window with animated blue balls. A list with a search box and some favorites would do the job, or better, connect always using the line command, IP or name assigned by the user.
16) Once you scan a server and it reveals other computers connected to that, more "balls" appears and its a mystery why some are very distant and some are very close. The distance is based on what? It simple confuses the player as it adds a connection between them and with time the connections cross each other. Well, still trying to figure out why did it this way.
17) I'm already playing this game for hours and all I do is execute programs to open ports.


The good:

a) Very well done interface in the sense that keyboard and mouse usage is well integrated. The key here is keyboard. Its very nice to be able to play the entire game using keyboard only.
b) I like the fact that webserver have website with real images. Just because its a hacker game, it doesn't mean the "normal" internet doesn't exist. Although limited, I liked the www.cfc.com.
c) You can see an effort to bring interesting content to see around. Most servers have files that are not crucial to the missions, things you can read, chats, funny stuff. That really adds to the game and was one of the things I feel lacking in Uplink. Perhaps this is one of the reason a lot of servers don't have tracing mechanism, so you don't have time pressure all the time.
d) Not having time pressure all the time is good, but also removed money pressure and other stuff, which is left it a bit unbalanced.
e) Nice animations. The screens change a lot. Its not the same interface all the time.

Just a window with animated blue balls. A list with a search box and some favorites would do the job, or better, connect always using the line command, IP or name assigned by the user. 16) Once you scan a server and it reveals other computers connected to that, more "balls" appears and its a mystery why some are very distant and some are very close. The screens change a lot. Its not the same interface all the time.

This is an extremely fun game, don't get me wrong, but I have two very major issues with it (especially the second one) that have prompted me to leave a negative review.  I very rarely review games on Steam, and only review the ones about which I am most passionately moved, positively or negatively.  In this case, negatively.  In contrast to my usual, I have enabled comments on this review -- feel free to state your feedback, whether you agree with me or not, just please remain respectful to me, the developers, other commenters, and anyone else as applicable.

There's a "TL;DR" at the end if you're lazy.

I'll start positive.  This game is crazy fun.  It is probably the funnest hacking-themed game I've ever played, and I've played a lot of them.  It was fun and helpful to see some things I recognize from real life, such as the default system port numbers being accurate and the existence of a few UNIX commands (my main OS has been FreeBSD for years, and my experience with UNIX helped with the gameplay in a way that felt good).  I liked seeing the C# source code and realizing it was actual, real C# source code that would probably work if the LESS_THAN was properly changed to a "<" sign, etc (C# is my main dev language, always a plus to see it referenced in a game at all).  That was cool, and I'll probably compile it later to have that tool on my PC for real (don't comment about the related real life security to this -- I assure you I already know, and it's just for fun).  The pacing was really good, and I got hooked fast.  So fast that I immediately bought the DLC, soundtrack, and DLC soundtrack for myself, then bought the game and DLC for both my wife and her boyfriend also.  Despite my negative review, I don't regret this decision at all, it's a very, very fun game.  Oh, the event thing that I can't discuss without giving spoilers, but well, the one where you need to get that thing back, that was super fun!  (Unimportant to the review and a spoiler:) I instinctively [spoiler]jumped to my host and forkbombed, apparently I was supposed to kill his forkbomb instead, oh well... I had already made a backup of that file just in case[/spoiler].  But anyway, the game was extremely fun, looks great, the music is great, and I'm excited to keep playing and see where things take me.

But there are two issues which were severe enough that they prompted me to leave a negative review despite all this.

The first issue isn't so bad and is easily rectified: This game is the pinnacle of Hollywood-style hacking.  It does it very well, and it references real hacking concepts in the game's flavor text and other areas.  Some tools are named the same as real ones, and you will probably learn a few real UNIX system port numbers, but that's about where the realism ends.  Oh, and [b]this wouldn't bother me in the slightest[/b] -- I love Hollywood-style hacking sim games! -- but it clearly says this in the "Features" section in the game's Steam page description, which to me is [u]blatant false advertisement[/u]:

[quote]
Real Hacking
Based on actual UNIX commands, Hacknet focuses on real hacking, not the Hollywood-style version of it.
[/quote]

If I stated what I consider my qualifications for knowing what constitutes "Hollywood-style" hacking, nobody would believe me, so I won't.  But even if you have never seen either a vtty or Hackers, I feel like anyone looking at the animation for the command called "porthack", god and the command name itself, and how it works, and everything related to the actual process of hacking (kinda the core concept in the entire game)... well I just think it doesn't take an expert to realize it's about as unrealistic as you can get.  If you don't believe me and this matters to you, buy the game and try it.  You will know I'm right within the 2 hour window to return it for a full refund, I assure you.  There is no "SSHCrack", no "FTPBounce", these wouldn't be PE executables if they did exist, PE doesn't even run on UNIX, "opening ports" and having requirements for a certain arbitrary number of open ports to "porthack" is very Hollywood.  Stahp.  Hollywood-style hacking is fine, don't be ashamed of it!  But most importantly, [b]advertise this game for it's many strengths, not for a falsehood[/b].  This game doesn't need lies to make it sound good, it's already a good game.  It's already a [i]great[/i] game.  Don't make false claims that sour its image.

Ok, now for the big one (to me).  Some people, many perhaps, won't care about this but I care.  I am quite literally sick to my stomach right now.  This has perhaps very minor spoilers for a very small number of optional (so far where I am in the story) missions, so I will spoiler-tag a lot to be safe, but even if you haven't played the game and hate spoilers, you probably won't be upset for reading the spoiler-tagged text in the next paragraph, it's the mildest of mild spoilers.

So, some of the missions require you to access a database of [spoiler]death row records[/spoiler] and modify them.  The missions are fine, and the topics are relevant.  I thought this was a positive thing to include in the game... until I gained access to this database and actually started reading the records.  I read about 40 of them in a row, unable to stop.  These were not made up, they were real records.  They had to be.  Surely the names were changed at least, right?  I Googled one at random and sure enough it was entirely real, and even the name, age, and date matched.  The [spoiler]last words[/spoiler] were their real [spoiler]last words[/spoiler], verbatim.  There is literally a massive database of actual real people's [spoiler]deaths[/spoiler] including their real [spoiler]last words[/spoiler] in the game, and there are missions to modify this database!  It is making light of a very serious topic with real people's real, actual names, turning it into a game.  If I am [spoiler]executed[/spoiler], I don't want my [spoiler]last words[/spoiler] to be made into a fun, "cool" game.  That's awful!  These families are mourning!  Please do not take real, actual tragedy and juxtapose it alongside comical IRC chat logs!  In a game?!  If you are a U.S. company, the families of these people may have legal justification to press charges.  I almost hope they do.  But instead of that, I would rather you modify your game and replace the real data with artificial data that you make up, or at least change the names and please also [spoiler]their last words[/spoiler].  This would have been such a cool set of missions, with a positive political message, but since you used real data it ruins the whole thing and instead makes it a mishandled slog of insensitivity... or... words, I just hate that you used real data for this.  Please replace it with artificial data.  It won't hurt the game.  It will take a single developer a day, if that, and then you can be on the right side of things, morally and honestly probably legally.  I plan to ask my lawyer his opinion on this sometime when he's not busy, not to press charges myself (I'm not listed in the data), but just out of legal curiosity if charges could be pressed for something like this.

Anyway this is a fun game and I'm not going to try to refund it, I'm not even going to stop playing it, but I will stop recommending it or buying it for more people (I have a tendency to buy games I like repeatedly for lots and lots of people, friends, family, etc.).  I think I bought Necesse 12 or 13 times?  I also fully plan to modify this review if my issues are addressed.  I will do so as soon as I notice the changes.  If you reply to this review when you've addressed them, I will likely notice faster and therefore update it faster... you know, if you don't want one nerd girl's negative review.

TL;DR: Great game, super fun.  But it uses false advertising on its Steam page, and is horribly insensitive to real mourning families IRL, and doesn't even change the names.

-- Amy

review_text_raw:
Hacknet is a rare gem in the indie scene—a game that doesn't just simulate hacking, but immerses you in it with a level of authenticity and atmosphere that most genre attempts barely graze. Designed by Team Fractal Alligator, it's a terminal-based hacking simulator where you dive deep into a rabbit hole of digital espionage, underground networks, and cryptic puzzles, all communicated through a command-line interface. On paper, that may sound dry. In execution, it’s anything but.

What makes Hacknet such a standout experience, is its faithfulness to real-world logic without alienating player unfamiliar with coding. It teaches by doing, never hand-holding but never abandoning you either. You’ll boot systems, probe for vulnerabilities, crack passwords, and manipulate files—all with just a blinking cursor and your wits. There’s a certain thrill in executing a flawless sequence of commands under pressure, like defusing a bomb with only seconds to spare.

The most positive  consistently praise its atmosphere. The soundtrack—moody and immersive—drenches every hack in tension and mystery. The narrative, while not overly complex, feeds a constant sense of curiosity. You're not just following orders; you're unraveling a digital conspiracy. Describe the experience as “empowering,” especially for those who’ve never touched a line of code before. There’s a genuine sense of growth as you become more fluent in your digital arsenal.

That said, even the best-crafted code has bugs. Point out a few frustrating limitations. First, while the UI is stylistically perfect for the theme, it can become visually fatiguing over long sessions, especially when you're staring at lines of text with minimal interface variety. Second, once you grasp the core mechanics, the challenge can taper off. Some missions fall into predictable patterns, and may find the mid-to-late game lacking in complexity.

Additionally, the lack of real choice in how you approach objectives can feel constricting. While it feels like a sandbox at first glance, the game often funnels you into single-solution puzzles. Wishing for more freedom to experiment or “break the system” in creative ways.

Hacknet is a brilliant idea executed with style, but not without cracks in its shell. The story is intriguing, yet occasionally shallow; the pacing tight, though at times undermined by repetitiveness. Still, it’s universally acknowledged as an educational and atmospheric triumph, especially for those willing to sink into its digital depths.

Final Verdict:
Hacknet is a thinking person’s game—a methodical, immersive dive into the world of virtual infiltration. It empowers through minimalism, teaches through tension, and wraps it all in a darkly ambient package. Despite a few structural shortcomings, it stands tall as a uniquely engrossing experience.

Rating: 8.5/10
A captivating digital puzzle-box, slightly constrained by its own structure, but well worth unlocking.

review_text_raw:
[h1] Many will claim that this is like playing the next version of Uplink since it is the most realistic hacking type game since Uplink was released. A very unique genre I think with very few games making a significant mark. I cannot claim to have played that classic so I will have to describe this entertaining game called Hacknet without any past comparisons. I will say that the reason it is compared though is because it takes the hacking seriously and isn't just some casual hacking game for the masses. [/h1]

Hacknet has almost no graphics (Maybe about 5 image files in the entire game), it has no video. It is only you looking at a computer screen full of numbers and files. You are a hacker, not Rambo, or James Bond, or Batman. You don't shoot at criminals and punch clowns in the face to save the day. You are a hacker that has found yourself in the middle of some hacking factions that may have stumbled into something big. You get some simple clues at the start that something is going on, but as you delve deeper into the hacking world, get recruited by more skillful hacking groups, and find more mysterious actions going on in your hacking exploits you will get asked to help find out what happened to a popular hacker that has gone missing. Just like everything in the hacking community, all useful information is hidden on systems which need to be hacked into. While looking for that information you will uncover many more secrets as you figure out exactly what happened. A final ending that could be considered a "shock". Very intriguing storyline and way to tell a story all through computer documents, e-mails, IRC chats, etc.

While the tutorials, and the game itself is friendly to those who have no experience entering command lines, or hacking at all, it may not exactly be for the most casual of gamers. If you are a VERY slow typist you may have some issues when it comes to hacking into computers here in the time frames that are allowed. They have made it easier for you by allowing you to hit "TAB" in certain places to have the game auto-complete command lines if there is nothing else that has the exact same characters and you are in the proper place to do so, however. It absolutely helps to have some typing speed, or at least the knowledge of where all the keys on the keyboard are without having to search them out all the time though. You will have issues if you are THAT slow.

You are tasked with finding various tools to run .exe files allowing you to open up ports on the computers you hack before running a PortHack program to get access to its files. Some computers early on are very easy to hack with only having to open 1-2 ports, but as you find more tools you may have to open as many as 5 ports, break through a firewall, and get through a proxy all on the same PC while avoiding a tracer too! So it becomes a bit quicker later on where you must know the commands and how to crack the security of various systems as the game progresses while fighting a clock too. You should pick up these skills as you play, but the knowledge of how to access certain databases will require a bit more thought at times. This is where the game adds a bit of strategy and puzzling into the mix. You need to think about what you are trying to do, search through maybe several other computers not just tools, but possibly passwords to OTHER computers, and even find ways to crack encrypted files! So it isn't always completely straightforward with the game holding your hand to get what you need. You will absolutely need to think somewhat critically here to reach your goals. IT is very refreshing to find a game that doesn't just offer you solutions on a silver platter and challenges you to figure things out yourself. It is quite rewarding in some cases to find a solution after thinking all your options through. Sometimes you can even find solutions to future problems by just HACKING into things you aren't even supposed to be working on for no other reason than because you felt like it.

Hacknet had a few bugs when I got it at release, but it appears that most have been taken care of. I finished the game, but I had a quest that didn't trigger properly so I had to hack my way around into other things to find the info I needed to proceed. Something that really wasn't that big a deal because it felt like I was actually doing something I figured out myself to get around a problem. The triggers have been patched now though as far as I know. Other than that nothing I ran into.

Hacknet does make you feel like a hacker if you have never done any hacking before in your life. It does use real world terminology and command lines to satisfy those that have in the past too so it isn't just for the hacker n00bs out there. The fast paced and tech-y music playing in the background was designed to make you feel like you are hacking systems as a hero in a movie. Punching in commands as fast you can can before getting caught is definitely helped by the pace of the music playing while you are trying to look into the dirty secrets of every computer you hack into.

I found Hacknet to be a fantastic feeling of hacking and mystery solving. While you may feel that the middle gets a little bit repetitive when it comes to the hacking, it does usually change up enough in what you need to use to keep the pacing OK. Usually what you find in the files, and of course the ending was payoff enough to continue through if you start to feel like you are staring at a flashing screen too long. I absolutely would not recommend this game to a casual gamer at all. Unlike say a point and click adventure, the puzzles you solve here will require quick thinking and quick fingers at times. Most players will be fine with this, but this is a game that require MUCH more activity on the keyboard than it does with a mouse. So you are typing commands for what you need to do in, and not using a mouse to solve puzzles as much. If you don't read the help files, the tutorial, and look at the academic databases in the game you will not be able to figure things out. If you want a brainless game this one is not for you.

The game has trading cards of course and Steam Achievements, which should be fairly easy to 100% if you can get through the game. This game should take you anywhere from 5-10 hours. More if you look around some and find every secret I suspect.

NOTE: Something I didn't talk about, because I am unsure what it consists of, is that Hacknet will be releasing a patch at some point that includes not just Steam Workshop to add more player made "questing", but it will also have Multiplayer! Like I said I don't know much about those aspects, but they are definitely coming. MP was in the game before Steam so it already exists, but the developers didn't feel it was working well enough yet to release with the Steam release. They wanted to stamp out any single player bugs first before bringing in these other features.

review_text_raw:
I'd only recommend this game if: you get it for free or really cheap, you want a short game to play but don't care what, or you just really want to see lots of scrolling lines and feel like a faux hacker

Otherwise, I don't think it's worth your time for the following reasons:

1. too simple and repetitive
Once you figure out the command lines after a few minutes that's the entire game play. In fact, you'll have to type the same things over so many times you'll mostly use the GUI menu instead. Then, you just wait around all the time waiting for the same 4-5 port hacks to finish that's nothing more than progress bars and flashing numbers like you see in movies. You do this again and again over the next few hours doing simple contracts you pick up from the hacker group postings board (which don't require any thinking since they tell you exactly where to go and what to do which is most of the time just deleting some files off the target server). 

2. lack of story and immersion
As mentioned above, 90% of the time you are doing these simple job postings. The other 10% is the actual story but other than a quick introduction to the missing dead hacker in the beginning, all of its related missions are shoehorned at the end in like the last three missions. Also, another problem I had was the immersion. If you read the files in the folders they want you to target, they're related to the back story of the mission you're doing but if you poke around in the home folder they're just a bunch of random files. For example, it doesn't make sense to read irc chat logs of teenagers making dumb pun jokes and a grocery list in an enterprise server.

3. some poor ui choices
Every IP address you visit is pinned on a board as a node that you can revisit at anytime. However, the nodes become very cluttered towards the end of the game, and critical story nodes at the end are overlapped with a bunch of nodes you visited at the start of the game. I got stuck for a bit for one mission because when I scanned for connected networks I could not see the one out of the five that newly showed up which I needed to go to. It really didn't help that the countdown timer (active trace, which I'll talk about below) was right on top of that region, blocking my view. Lastly, there's something about the background and font color choice and or the font size that is eye straining and made me feel nauseous at times. Made me want to skim through the text a lot of the times.

4. feature bypass/abuse
There's a gameplay feature called active trace which is basically a countdown timer before the server tracks you down because it knows it's being hacked. Fun idea in theory but it's only ever a threat once in the game. Every other time you can circumvent it by hacking the server then disconnecting, then when you reconnect you can login as admin because it saved the password somehow from just hacking the ports. At this point you can leisurely scroll through the server and not worry about getting caught. If you do run out the timer and get caught you go into fail safe mode where you have a limited time to change your ip address but I just rebooted the virtual OS and that "solves" the problem.

rm *   --remove all files in directory
dc   --disconnect from server
shell    --create tool to hack proxies and trap hackers
reboot   --reboots server
analyze   --analyzes firewall, next command cracks it
solve <password>
porthack  --crack ports 
webserverworm 80   --crack HTTP port
smtpoverflow 25   --crack SMTP port
ftpbounce 21   --crack FTP port
sql_memcorrupt 1433  --crack SQL port
sshcrack  -- crack SSH port

Need to get rid of Proxy server? connect to a different IP address where you have admin privs and type shell. You can now go back to the IP address you want to hack and click overlog in your left or right panel, next to your notes.

Use ls to see your log files.
Find the IP address that hacked you and type connect followed by that IP address.
You are now going to use probe as usual to begin hacking the computer.
Run SSHCrack and PortHack.
Use cd to go into the sys folder.
Use ls and you will see he has a system file there for you to use to fix your computer.
Type scp x-server.sys to copy the system file to your computer.
Use dc to get back to your computer.
Type reboot

Many will claim that this is like playing the next version of Uplink since it is the most realistic hacking type game since Uplink was released. A very cult genre I think with very few games making a significant mark. I cannot claim to have played that classic so I will have to describe this entertaining game called Hacknet without any past comparisons. I will say that the reason it is compared though is because it takes the hacking seriously and isn't just some casual hacking game for the masses. 

Hacknet has almost no graphics (Maybe about 5 image files in the entire game), it has no video. It is only you looking at a computer screen full of numbers and files. You are a hacker, not Rambo, or James Bond, or Batman. You don't shoot at criminals and punch clowns in the face to save the day. You are a hacker that has found yourself in the middle of some hacking factions that may have stumbled into something big. You get some simple clues at the start that something is going on, but as you delve deeper into the hacking world, get recruited by more skillful hacking groups, and find more mysterious actions going on in your hacking exploits you will get asked to help find out what happened to a popular hacker that has gone missing. Just like everything in the hacking community, all useful information is hidden on systems which need to be hacked into. While looking for that information you will uncover many more secrets as you figure out exactly what happened. A final ending that could be considered a "shock". Very intriguing storyline and way to tell a story all through computer documents, e-mails, IRC chats, etc. 

While the tutorials, and the game itself is friendly to those who have no experience entering command lines, or hacking at all, it may not exactly be for the most casual of gamers. If you are a VERY slow typist you may have some issues when it comes to hacking into computers here in the time frames that are allowed. They have made it easier for you by allowing you to hit "TAB" in certain places to have the game auto-complete command lines if there is nothing else that has the exact same characters and you are in the proper place to do so, however. It absolutely helps to have some typing speed, or at least the knowledge of where all the keys on the keyboard are without having to search them out all the time though. You will have issues if you are THAT slow.  

You are tasked with finding various tools to run .exe files allowing you to open up ports on the computers you hack before running a PortHack program to get access to its files. Some computers early on are very easy to hack with only having to open 1-2 ports, but as you find more tools you may have to open as many as 5 ports, break through a firewall, and get through a proxy all on the same PC while avoiding a tracer too! So it becomes a bit quicker later on where you must know the commands and how to crack the security of various systems as the game progresses while fighting a clock too. You should pick up these skills as you play, but the knowledge of how to access certain databases will require a bit more thought at times. This is where the game adds a bit of strategy and puzzling into the mix. You need to think about what you are trying to do, search through maybe several other computers not just tools, but possibly passwords to OTHER computers, and even find ways to crack encrypted files! So it isn't always completely straightforward with the game holding your hand to get what you need. You will absolutely need to think somewhat critically here to reach your goals. IT is very refreshing to find a game that doesn't just offer you solutions on a silver platter and challenges you to figure things out yourself. It is quite rewarding in some cases to find a solution after thinking all your options through. Sometimes you can even find solutions to future problems by just HACKING into things you aren't even supposed to be working on for no other reason than because you felt like it. 

Hacknet had a few bugs when I got it at release, but it appears that most have been taken care of. I finished the game, but I had a quest that didn't trigger properly so I had to hack my way around into other things to find the info I needed to proceed. Something that really wasn't that big a deal because it felt like I was actually doing something I figured out myself to get around a problem. The triggers have been patched now though as far as I know. Other than that nothing I ran into. 

Hacknet does make you feel like a hacker if you have never done any hacking before in your life. It does use real world terminology and command lines to satisfy those that have in the past too so it isn't just for the hacker n00bs out there. The fast paced and tech-y music playing in the background was designed to make you feel like you are hacking systems as a hero in a movie. Punching in commands as fast you can can before getting caught is definitely helped by the pace of the music playing while you are trying to look into the dirty secrets of every computer you hack into. 

I found Hacknet to be a fantastic feeling of hacking and mystery solving. While you may feel that the middle gets a little bit repetitive when it comes to the hacking, it does usually change up enough in what you need to use to keep the pacing OK. Usually what you find in the files, and of course the ending was payoff enough to continue through if you start to feel like you are staring at a flashing screen too long. I absolutely would not recommend this game to a casual gamer at all. Unlike say a point and click adventure, the puzzles you solve here will require quick thinking and quick fingers at times. Most players will be fine with this, but this is a game that require MUCH more activity on the keyboard than it does with a mouse. So you are typing commands for what you need to do in, and not using a mouse to solve puzzles as much. If you don't read the help files, the tutorial, and look at the academic databases in the game you will not be able to figure things out. If you want a brainless game this one is not for you.

The game has trading cards of course and Steam Achievements, which should be fairly easy to 100% if you can get through the game. This game should take you anywhere from 5-10 hours. More if you look ar ound some and find every secret I suspect.

NOTE: Something I didn't talk about, because I am unsure what it consists of, is that Hacknet will be releasing a patch at some point that includes not just Steam Workshop to add more player made "questing", but it will also have Multiplayer! Like I said I don't know much about those aspects, but they are definitely coming. MP was in the game before Steam so it already exists, but the developers didn't feel it was working well enough yet to release with the Steam release. They wanted to stamp out any single player bugs first before bringing in these other features.

It is difficult to make a game that captures the feel of hacking. A hacker is successful because he has a large body of knowledge to pull from. He tries a thousand different things before something works.

Making an exciting game about hacking is like making an exciting game about coming up with new mathematical theorems. 

Hacknet is far more fun that I expected, but that isn't saying much. You are given four or five scripts to run with various levels of time pressure. There is a lot of good flavor, being able to customize your UI, using a simplified UNIX, and accessing system files.

Sadly, the gameplay wasn't enough to keep me playing and the story, while interesting, wasn't original enough to carry the game.

For a more detailed review of this and other Steam games I bought for cheap, check out my blog:

Hacknet is a unique and immersive hacking simulator that manages to blend educational elements with engaging gameplay to deliver an experience that feels both authentic and accessible. Developed by Team Fractal Alligator, the game places players in the role of a recently deceased hacker whose death was mysteriously logged in the system, prompting you to follow their digital footsteps through a series of hacking tasks. From the moment you begin, Hacknet pulls you into a gritty, text-based cyber world that relies heavily on realistic command-line interfaces, compelling storytelling, and a sense of discovery that is rarely found in traditional puzzle or adventure games.

At its core, Hacknet is all about learning and using real-world hacking concepts in a fictional setting. The gameplay revolves around typing actual Unix-based commands, running scripts, cracking passwords, and exploiting network vulnerabilities. Unlike many games that simplify hacking into a series of quick minigames or button presses, Hacknet demands attention to detail and encourages experimentation. The command line interface is intuitive yet detailed, and the game introduces commands gradually, allowing players to build a solid understanding of the mechanics as they progress. The pacing strikes a perfect balance between tutorialization and challenge, making it approachable for newcomers without feeling watered down for those with some technical knowledge.

The narrative is one of the standout features of Hacknet. It unfolds through in-game emails, chat logs, and system messages, painting a picture of a shadowy digital underworld filled with intrigue, moral ambiguity, and complex characters. You’re not just hacking for the sake of hacking; there is an overarching mystery and a compelling story that motivates your actions. The writing is sharp, immersive, and at times surprisingly emotional, which elevates the experience beyond a purely mechanical simulation. The game’s episodic structure ensures that the story unfolds organically, revealing new layers and twists as you delve deeper into the cyber realm.

review_text_raw:
Hacknet is pretty much what it says on the tin - a hacking-themed game in which you must meet escalating challenges throughout the course of its story, which opens with a posthumous message coming from a hacker who has disappeared.  Stop right there, though - the story isn't very strong on the conspiracy and ends up being a missed opportunity, so don't dive in just yet.

Those not familiar with command-lines need not fret as this isn't a full-blown OS simulator like other games in the genre.  While it does have its own level of CLI sophistication, the tutorial and pacing thereafter is carefully crafted as not to overwhelm the inexperienced.  Anyone looking to roleplay a super hacking machine can comfortably play this game without having a manual in front of them (though a notepad may help).  Rather than have you coding a bunch of exploits or what have you, your hacking terminal - which is beautifully-rendered, btw - is loaded with magical tools that do all the work for you.  You just need to handle the set up, if you will, and the software will do the rest.

What separates Hacknet from others in the genre is its combo of command-line terminal and graphical user interface (think X-Window).  The game is aesthetically pleasing to the eye with a mix of hi- and low-tech, giving the interface an authentic OS feel.  If you're not keen on typing every little thing (which you can absolutely elect to do), you can instead click on the GUI to navigate around most of the systems and poke around.  You'll still need to key in some commands, but there's a good balance here if you want to save some time with navigation and reading files.  Websites aren't functional, but they do appear in the game and give it that extra little flavor, with one exception being a Clicker game that you can waste time on should you so choose to.

So while the story doesn't really play out in the best of ways, the hacking is quite fun... at least for the first little bit.  It very soon becomes repetitive because ultimately the puzzles are limited.  You will be taking on contracts/jobs from message servers and they each boil down to a) get into the target system and b) grab some information or delete stuff.  Even though you are introduced to new tools (and thus, the difficulty of breaking into a system increases), the game rarely deviates from this formula, even when the story demands it.  It's not really until the latter quarter of the game when you're doing interesting stuff, not so much because the repetitiveness is gone, but more because the answers aren't quite as obvious.

I would have liked to have a more involved tale form throughout the game and as I said above, it's a missed opportunity.  It would make discovery so much more satisfying.  This isn't made much better by most servers being devoid of anything interesting other than some randomly-pulled bash quotes which, if you've been around on the Internet long enough, you've already read.  Still, this is a minor nitpick and beyond that, there was nary an issue with the game.  I encountered no bugs or crashes, except that I wasted a good 2 or 3 hours trying to go down a different path (which happens under very, very specific circumstances), which highlighted the inability to save-where-you-want; basically, failing to meet the conditions, even though I thought I knew what I had to do, meant that I had to restart from scratch repeatedly just to get there... however, this alternate path is completely optional and easily-missed.  I only put this here as a warning to achievement hunters.

At the end of the day, Hacknet is a fun game that captures the spirit of hacking without overwhelming the player.  I'm sure there are more hardcore games in the genre, but at that point - in my opinion - I feel it stops being a game and starts being a job.  Hacknet manages to find the right balance between authenticity and Hollywood fantasy so it's a very enjoyable experience.

Just be aware that the blue screens look incredibly authentic.  Don't panic.

Having just completed the main campaign at the time of writing - with an expansion DLC and community-made storylines to go grab whenever I fancy - I find myself applauding a demonstrable, confident and competent passion project.

Sitting at a fake operating system staring at flickering text and pondering what move to try next has no right to be this satisfying, yet Hacknet remains - with very few exceptions - a title that rewards ingenuity, curiosity and player agency. People say this is one of the definitive hacking simulators, and if this is indeed the case, it's not just the fact that you can screw around so intensively in a simulated internet ecosystem that you actually break the plot - it's because you're doing what hackers actually do most of the time, which is sit back, let out a big puffy-cheek sigh of mild exasperation and mutter "ugh, how do we get around THAT one?!" or "oh wow, I probably shouldn't have been able to do this yet am being rewarded for doing so."

The game teaches a few handy command line basics for those not in the know, but it's not going to give you much of anything in the way of dangerous IRL skills, largely because the premise of the game is that a fellow hacker has created a catch-all exploit that can open any computer like a can of sardines with the right complementary toolkit. Obtaining these tools, deepening your dive into the rabbithole and exploring a series of both serious and darkly comical scenarios is very much the crux of the game, and it's enjoyable and often tense in ways simply sitting at a computer has no right to be.

At the time of this review I have 10 hours in, and that's the core campaign done and dusted - enjoyable throughout and very rarely apt to let any pacing issues slip. Missions are unlocked by communicating with shady friends (and sometimes frenemies) who closely guard IP addresses and web tools that can expand your arsenal and uncover the truth behind those lurking in the darkest reaches of the web, trashing our rights man, TRAAAASHING.

Coupled with a banging soundtrack and just enough thrills and spills to make you sit up and pay attention when you get too cocky, Hacknet couples both careful thread-pulling at mysteries and intrigue with heartpounding oh-god-oh-dear-god panic moments where the screen goes weird and you know you're up a creek you were never invited to with a paddle your trembling fingers now can't spell the name of, just as you need it the most.

Excited to try community and DLC plotlines next!

Hacknet is probably one of my favorite lil hacker sims currently, I think it's great fun if you enjoy these types of games!! Downside is you can absolutely softlock yourself quite easy, so make sure to be cautious about what you delete and when, since some important info can be contained in logs or other assorted files. Highly recommended tho!!

Hacknet is largely terminal-based, and is pretty classic for this genre of game: you input various commands and poke around at other systems after hacking into them. There is also a more visual interface you can click around on if navigating purely via terminal is a bit rough for you, but there's a few sections of game that DO require you to only use the terminal, so I'd recommend getting used to it while you can. I come from a coding background so it's hard to say how intelligible this is if you don't have experience messing about with command prompts, but there are some tutorials present so I'm sure you could crack it even if you don't have the experience =)) You'll be digging around inside files for pertinent information, finding ways to mess with said files, delete them outright, or upload your own substitutes in order to complete quests for various factions and progress the story. 

Honestly, I really enjoyed all the hacking puzzles!! I think there's a good mixture of ones that're nice and easy to ease you into it as well as some that felt like they required a bit more digging and clever thinking. The DLC, Labyrinths, was also a pretty cohesive experience but it certainly expected you to have learned quite a bit from the base game so you could work very quickly. The time pressure can be quite real, so I hope you're a fast typer lol.

I ran into one main issue, which was in the DLC. There's a section that asks you to use the command prompt to delete a file, and it seems to be somewhat inconsistent if this works or not - so consider this a brief warning, and a bit of a cheat in case you need it: using your file explorer to delete the file that way seems to work completely fine as long as you have admin. Then validate game files and restart the game and you should be good to go!!

This game is on a whole new level. Not many ambitious games like this can simultaneously achieve what they were hoping for (a realistic hacking sim) and make it fundamentally a good standalone game. You could have an accurate farming simulator, but then fail to make it fun with poor progression and pacing, or vice versa. This game doesn't compromise; it does both and does them well.

So for the recommendation part, here's a quick list of the good and bad (minimal spoilers).

Pros: 
[list]
    [*] One of the most comprehensive/accurate hacking sim games out there (rejoice, UNIX users)
    [*] Designed for beginners and the experienced alike
    [*] Great music, atmosphere, story, and of course gameplay
    [*] Fun puzzles, with good but not overly instrusive prompts
    [*] Replayability with some randomisations (expect 2-5 playthroughs for non-DLC)
    [*] Multiple routes, and many secrets
    [*] Everything links to each other (secrets, stories/lore, hints,)
    [*] Great community and moderators, if you ever need help
[/list]

Cons:
[list]
    [*] Not all missions may have the best "turn-in" trigger hints, but you can always consult the friendly community
    [*] Due to the complexities of data sanitisation in a game like this, not "everything" is technically possible (you can still do some fun stuff, just not literal programming inside the files)
    [*] Possible to get softlocked in many places; just dont stray off too far off the course and rm * every server lol
    [*] Singleplayer, because multiplayer turned out to be overly amibtious (even for this dev) and severly was underplayed
    [*] Existance of an awesome GUI may break the illusion of a "truly accurate" hacking sim, making it seem more like a script kiddie simulator, but I think this is justified for keeping the game immersive and fun for everyone
[/list]

Afternotes:
I got this game for free and completed it on day one while exploring some secrets. No breakfast, no lunch, and no dinner until I had finished. The very next day I played it all over again two more times to explore every last secret. I didn't think I would say this for any game, but I'll definitely buy the DLC when I get the chance. It is really that good of a game.

In [i]Hacknet[/i], you play as a computer user who has just been bestowed a unique operating system (OS) with tools that can hack different computers. As the game progresses, you will discover new hacking tools, join other factions of hackers, fulfill hacking job contracts to build your reputation, and solve the game’s central mystery.

What I love about [i]Hacknet[/i] is the high level of immersion and engaging pacing. With my headphones on, listening to the adrenaline-pumping soundtrack, I voraciously took on one hacking contract after another. Before long, two to three hours have flown by. The game's missions, though all require hacking, vary in objects and pacing. Because of that, I did not find gameplay repetitive, and I used every opportunity to familiarize myself with the tools I had at my disposal. All of this prepared me for the climatic final mission, which totally did not disappoint.

[i]Hacknet[/i] is novice-friendly, but some players may find it having a slightly steep learning curve. Players will be at an advantage if they can type fast, has used *nix (e.g. Linux) shell commands, and/or are familiar with text-based OSes. This is because the user interface of [i]Hacknet[/i] is austere, with typing as your primary form of input. Still, there are simple graphics to depict hacking progress, network of computers, and directory trees. You can use your mouse from time to time as means of in-game navigation as I did.

[i]Hacknet[/i]'s appeal aside from immersion and pacing is really its simplicity. The players will always be given all the tools they would need to complete missions. So, the real challenge is to figure out which tool(s) to use to hack the computers and phones, and to do it quickly and efficiently. So, think fast! Type fast and furious! Once the dust has settled, snooping around the hacked machines and reaping your rewards are gratifying.

At the time of this review, [i]Hacknet[/i] is my favourite hacking-themed game. It’s fast, it’s empowering, and it’s extremely gratifying -- especially after a challenging mission. I highly recommend this game to those who wish an adrenaline-pumping, brain-teasing, text-based adventure game.

review_text_raw:
Probably the most fun you can legally have with directory commands. Still, Hacknet may or may not be for you, depending on what you're hoping to get out of it. 

If you're in it for the narrative experience and the voyeuristic joy of poking around in other people's business and/or places that you don't belong, indulging the cinematically-improbable-but-evergreen-cool Hacker Man(tm) in your heart to the appropriately driving beat of smooth EDM, then you'll definitely enjoy what this game is -- regardless of your actual level of familiarity with all things tech. It's a game that intends to be accessible so it glosses over the hard stuff, handing you tools that amount to pegs you've got to put into the proper holes at the proper time, often under (mild) time pressure. They're basic, familiar video game mechanics, dressed up this time as Hacker Stuff, and I think it works because it takes a back seat to the story. The game doesn't take itself too seriously, but has poignant moments all the same. 

If what you want instead is a game that's going to have you actually writing code or cracking difficult puzzles, this isn't what you're looking for. The guy who made it clearly has a background in tech, but this isn't a Zachtronics thing -- it's essentially a slick visual novel with some fun exploratory/investigative elements and some hidden surprises for diligent snoopers.

I was excited to see that other people have crafted their own bite-sized stories for Hacknet, and I'm looking forward to trying them out!

SPANDEX IS A PRIVILEGE, BUT THIS TERMINAL IS A BIRTHRIGHT

Yo! Grab your Jolt Cola, slap on your rollerblades, and look at the screen! Look at it!

Most games hand you a plastic neon toy and call it "cyberpunk." Not Hacknet. This isn't some baby-town Hollywood nonsense where mash-keys-to-win happens. This is the digital slipstream!

1. An Elite Adventure: It starts with a dead hacker’s automated distress beacon and spirals into pure, adrenaline-soaked corporate espionage. It’s an actual mystery with real stakes, paranoia, and elite-tier narrative hacking. You aren't just playing; you’re unraveling a digital ghost story.

2. Streamlined for Maximum Rush: Yeah, some commands and mechanics are streamlined so you aren't stuck reading 80-page manual dumps just to crack a port. The pacing moves at lightspeed to keep the thrill alive, but the logic remains authentic and deeply satisfying.

3. Mouse for Casuals, CLI for Gods: You can point-and-click your little desktop GUI like a tourist, or you can live where the legends live: 100% in the command line. Manually hammering out cat, rm *, nmap, and porthack while the system countdown timers bleed red neon makes you feel like you just bypassed the Gibson.

4. Pure Flow State: The soundtrack bumps, the text logs are fascinating to dig through, and when you execute a clean sweep without leaving a single trace, you will want to scream HACK THE PLANET!

It’s smart, thrilling, and an absolute blast of an adventure.

10/10. Zeroes and ones, baby. Zeroes and ones!

review_text_raw:
A fun game that makes you feel like a hacker. 

The internal logic of the game is really good, and the game does offer some possibility of mastery.

The pacing is actually EXCELLENT and something that a lot of games like this get wrong: it teaches the player the mechanics and scales up the difficulty in a really nice way. 

For people unfamiliar with computers and UNIX systems, this is a great entryway into learning the basics of navigation, and also mimics some of the conceptual problemsolving skills one needs to be a hacker.

There were times that I was overthinking problems, and most of the time the game simply requires you to "search and find the answer" rather than figure out a more complex sollution, though there are a couple of paths in the game that allows you to flex your skills and challenges you if you're up to it.

The story and writing is trying to punch above its weight but it serves its purpose. Sometimes it got a chuckle out of me, and it was fun to dig through files and find some silly conversations. But its a tad cliche, even for 2013. The plot allows you to live out the fantasy within the limitations and rules of the game mechanics, so its effective but not groundbreaking.

Overall the best OS-simulator "hacker" game I've played so far.

It is also helpful to write down some of the commands you learn or to follow a guide along the way in case you get stuck (which happened to me a few times). The writing uses humor and some tense timed moments to keep things interesting. Overall, I enjoyed this quite a lot and would recommend it.
